title: The Human Respiratory System: A Guided Journey
subject: Biology
summary: Follow one breath from the nose to the alveoli and into your cells. At each of nine stops, predict which parts, features, processes and molecules are involved, explain it aloud, then see what really happens, including how oxygen and carbon dioxide swap places in the blood.

groups.question: Which parts of the body are involved?
Which features or structures do the work?

processes.label: Air passes through a shared route with food
Air spreads into ever smaller tubes
Anaerobic respiration with insufficient air: lactic acid forms
Anaerobic respiration with no air: alcohol and carbon dioxide form

checkpoints.prompt: You are at the entrance of the respiratory system. What happens to the air here? Why is it important that the air is warmed and filtered?
checkpoints.target: Warming, moistening and filtering the air
checkpoints.revealExplanation: Air enters through the nostrils, where nasal hairs trap the biggest dust particles. In the nasal cavity, the lining makes sticky mucus that traps dust, pollen and germs, and cilia (tiny hairs) sweep the mucus back to the throat to be swallowed. A rich supply of blood capillaries warms the air to body temperature and the moist lining adds water vapour, so delicate lung tissue is protected from cold, dry, dirty air.

checkpoints.prompt: The air now reaches the throat, a route that food also uses. What is this tube called, and what stops food from going down the windpipe?
checkpoints.target: A shared route for air and food
checkpoints.revealExplanation: The pharynx (throat) is a shared passage for air and food. Air flows from the nasal cavity through the pharynx down to the larynx. When you swallow, a flap called the epiglottis folds down over the entrance of the larynx so that food slides into the oesophagus instead of the windpipe.

checkpoints.prompt: You have reached the voice box and the windpipe. What happens at the larynx? What is the role of the rings around the trachea?
checkpoints.target: Sound production and a windpipe that stays open
checkpoints.revealExplanation: The larynx (voice box) holds the vocal cords. Air passing between them makes them vibrate, producing sound. Below it, the trachea (windpipe) is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage, so it does not collapse when air pressure changes during breathing. The open side of each C lets food pass down the oesophagus behind it, and the trachea's lining of mucus and cilia keeps sweeping dust upwards.

checkpoints.prompt: The windpipe now splits in two. What are these two main tubes called, and how do they carry on dividing as they go deeper into the lungs?
checkpoints.target: Air spreading to every part of the lungs
checkpoints.revealExplanation: The trachea divides into two bronchi, one for each lung. Inside the lungs each bronchus branches again and again into narrower bronchioles, like an upside-down tree, carrying air to every part of the lung. Bronchi are supported by cartilage, but bronchioles have none and instead have smooth muscle that can narrow them, as in an asthma attack. Each bronchiole ends in a cluster of tiny air sacs called alveoli.

checkpoints.prompt: You are inside the chest. The lungs fill most of it. What are they like, how are they protected, and why do they need so much inside space?
checkpoints.target: Spongy, protected organs built for a huge surface area
checkpoints.revealExplanation: The lungs are two soft, spongy, elastic organs protected by the rib cage. The right lung has three lobes and the left has two, leaving room for the heart. Each lung is wrapped in two pleural membranes with a thin film of fluid between them, so the lungs slide smoothly as they expand and recoil. Inside, hundreds of millions of alveoli give a huge surface area, around 70 square metres, for exchanging gases.

checkpoints.prompt: You have shrunk to the size of a molecule at the end of a bronchiole. What are these tiny air sacs called? How do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross between the air and the blood, and why are the walls built the way they are?
checkpoints.target: External respiration: gas exchange by diffusion
checkpoints.revealExplanation: This is external respiration: the exchange of gases between the air in the alveoli and the blood. Each alveolus has a wall only one cell thick and is wrapped in a net of capillaries. Oxygen is more concentrated in the alveolus than in the blood, so it diffuses into the blood and is picked up by haemoglobin in red blood cells. Carbon dioxide is more concentrated in the blood, so it diffuses out into the alveolus and is breathed out. Thin, moist walls and a huge surface area make this fast.

checkpoints.prompt: Breathing is a mechanical process. What happens to the diaphragm and rib cage when you inhale, and how does this draw air into the lungs?
checkpoints.revealExplanation: Breathing is a mechanical process, also called external respiration when we include the gas exchange it makes possible. To inhale, the diaphragm contracts and flattens downwards while the intercostal muscles lift the rib cage up and out. The volume of the chest increases, so the pressure inside the lungs drops below the outside pressure and air rushes in. To exhale, the diaphragm and intercostals relax, the diaphragm domes upwards and the ribs drop; the volume falls, the pressure rises and air is pushed out.

checkpoints.prompt: The blood has delivered oxygen to a body cell. What do we call the process in which cells use oxygen to release energy from food? Where in the cell does it happen, and what are the products?
checkpoints.target: Internal respiration releasing energy from glucose
checkpoints.revealExplanation: This is internal (cellular) respiration. Inside the mitochondria of every cell, glucose is broken down using oxygen to release energy: glucose + oxygen gives carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP). The carbon dioxide travels back in the blood to the lungs to be breathed out, and the energy powers movement, growth and body warmth. Because it uses oxygen, this is aerobic respiration, the most efficient of the three modes.

checkpoints.prompt: Sometimes cells cannot get enough oxygen. What happens in your muscles during a hard sprint when oxygen is short? What do yeast cells do when there is no air at all? How much energy is released compared with aerobic respiration?
checkpoints.target: Anaerobic respiration: lactic acid in muscles, alcohol in yeast
checkpoints.revealExplanation: There are three modes of respiration. Aerobic respiration uses plenty of oxygen: glucose is fully broken down into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a lot of energy. Anaerobic respiration with insufficient air happens in your muscles during hard exercise: glucose is only partly broken down into lactic acid and much less energy is released; the lactic acid builds up and makes the muscles ache and feel sour. Anaerobic respiration with no air at all happens in yeast: glucose is fermented into ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide, again releasing little energy. This is how bread dough rises and how alcohol is brewed.

scenarios.question: A smoker's cilia are damaged by smoke. What is the most direct result?

options.label: Mucus carrying dust and germs is not swept out, so it collects in the airways
The alveolar walls become thicker at once
The diaphragm cannot contract
Oxygen can no longer dissolve in blood

scenarios.explanation: Cilia sweep mucus and trapped particles up and out of the airways. When smoke paralyses them, the dirty mucus stays, causing 'smoker's cough' and infections.

scenarios.question: During an asthma attack the bronchioles narrow. What happens?

options.label: Less air reaches the alveoli, so breathing becomes difficult
The vocal cords stop vibrating
The cartilage rings in the trachea collapse
The diaphragm moves upwards when you inhale

scenarios.explanation: Narrow bronchioles let less air through, so less oxygen reaches the alveoli and the person struggles to breathe in and out.

scenarios.question: The diaphragm cannot contract. What is directly affected?

options.label: The chest cannot enlarge enough to draw air in
Cilia stop moving in the nose
Haemoglobin stops carrying oxygen
Cells switch to fermentation with ethanol

scenarios.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm increases chest volume and lowers the pressure inside the lungs. Without it, far less air is drawn in.

scenarios.question: A disease breaks down the walls of the alveoli, leaving fewer, bigger air sacs. What is reduced?

options.label: The surface area for gas exchange
The number of cartilage rings
The size of the nostrils
The fluid between the pleura

scenarios.explanation: Fewer, larger air sacs mean far less surface area for oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse across.

scenarios.question: A sprinter's muscles run short of oxygen. What builds up in the muscles?

options.label: Lactic acid
Ethanol (alcohol)
Extra oxygen
Starch

scenarios.explanation: With insufficient oxygen, muscle cells respire anaerobically, partly breaking down glucose into lactic acid and releasing much less energy.

scenarios.question: Bread dough has no air inside, yet it rises when yeast is added. Why?

options.label: Yeast respire anaerobically and release carbon dioxide gas
Yeast produce lactic acid, which swells the dough
Yeast use oxygen to make water
Yeast absorb carbon dioxide from the dough

scenarios.explanation: With no air, yeast ferment glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The gas bubbles make the dough rise.

scenarios.question: Which statement is correct?

options.label: External respiration is breathing and gas exchange in the lungs; internal respiration is the release of energy in cells
External respiration happens in the cells; internal respiration is breathing
Both words mean only breathing in and out
Respiration means the same as breathing and nothing else

scenarios.explanation: Breathing and gas exchange in the lungs are external respiration. Using oxygen to release energy from glucose inside cells is internal (cellular) respiration.

scenarios.question: Which mode of respiration releases the most energy from each molecule of glucose?

options.label: Aerobic respiration (with oxygen)
Anaerobic respiration in muscles
Anaerobic respiration in yeast
They all release exactly the same

scenarios.explanation: Aerobic respiration breaks glucose down completely into carbon dioxide and water, releasing far more energy than either anaerobic mode.

finalExplain.prompt: You are back at the nose. In your own words, explain the whole journey of an oxygen molecule from the nose to the alveoli and on to a body cell, and how the diaphragm drives breathing.
finalExplain.modelAnswer: Oxygen enters through the nose, where hairs, mucus and cilia filter the air and the nasal cavity warms and moistens it. It passes through the pharynx and the larynx into the trachea, which is held open by cartilage rings, then down a bronchus and along narrower bronchioles to an alveolus. There it diffuses across the one-cell-thick wall into the blood and is carried by haemoglobin to the body cells, where it is used in the mitochondria to release energy from glucose (internal respiration), while carbon dioxide travels back the other way. All of this is driven by the diaphragm: when it contracts and flattens and the ribs lift, the chest volume rises and the pressure drops, so air flows in.
